tales.title: How State Street was moved
text: Ten years ago nobody who mattered did business on State Street. Lake Street was the street: the wholesale houses, the dry goods, the banks a step away. State was a narrow muddy lane of frame shops and boarding houses.

Then Potter Palmer bought it. Not all of it, but near a mile of frontage, and he widened it, and he built a marble store at Washington and let it to Field and Leiter, and he has just opened a hotel at Monroe that he says is the finest in the West. Two weeks it has been open. Every merchant on Lake Street laughed at him and every one of them is looking for a lease on State now. One man moved a street. That is Chicago.

tales.title: Not a drop since July
text: Do you know when it last rained properly? The fourth of July. An inch since, maybe, and it has been hot and blowing out of the southwest for weeks. The leaves came down dry in September before they had turned. The pine sidewalks curl at the ends, the roofs are tar and shingle, and there is a lumber yard on every bend of the river.

There were twenty fire alarms last week, the papers say, and one of them burned four blocks on the West Side last night. The engines are worn out and so are the men. I am not a nervous man. But I have put the deed box by the door.

tales.title: Under the river
text: Have you been through the LaSalle Street tunnel? It opened this summer. You go down a ramp on the South Side, under the river, and up on the North Side, and the bridge can swing for a schooner all day and you never wait. There is a walk for foot passengers beside the carriage way, lit by gas.

The Washington Street one has been open two years on the West Side. It leaked, and the papers made fun of it, but it works. In the old days half your life in this city was spent standing at a swung bridge watching the masts go by. Now the river is a thing you go under.

tales.title: The year they lifted the city
text: When I came here the streets were at the lake's level and every spring they were a swamp. So the council raised the grade, four feet, eight feet, ten in places, and every man had to raise his house to meet it or live in a pit.

They jacked up the Tremont House, brick and all, with the guests still in it, and nobody spilled his coffee. That is why you will see a walk on one block a step higher than the next, and stairs up and down to the doors. Half the city is still not level with the other half. Mind your feet on the planks.

tales.title: Clean water from two miles out
text: You remember the water? We used to get fish in it. Little ones, out of the tap. The intake was at the shore where the river came out into the lake, and you can guess what the river carries.

So they dug a tunnel two miles under the lake to a crib out in clean water and built the pumping house and that tower on the North Side, with the standpipe inside it. The tower looks like a castle out of a picture book. The water comes in clear now. The children think it was always so.

tales.title: The river runs backwards
text: This summer they finished the deep cut on the canal and the river turned round. It used to run into the lake and take every slaughterhouse's leavings with it, out to where we drank. Now the canal pulls it the other way, down toward the Illinois.

I did not believe it until I stood on the Rush Street bridge and watched a stick float west. The smell on the South Branch is still bad, mind. They say it is better than it was. Everyone who says so lives on the North Side.

tales.title: The Sunday promenade
text: After dinner on a fine Sunday everybody walks. Michigan Avenue if you have a new bonnet, Wabash if you want to be seen without seeming to want it, the lake front if the children must run.

I wore the purple today. My husband says it is the colour of a bruise. My dressmaker says it is the colour of Paris. I have walked from Monroe to Twelfth and back and counted three other ladies in it, which my husband says proves his point and I say proves mine.

tales.title: The marble palace
text: Field and Leiter's store at State and Washington is six storeys of white marble with plate glass you could walk through if you were not careful. The clerks are young men in black coats who call you madam and bring the silks down for you one bolt at a time.

It is shut today, of course. But I walked past it after church to look in the windows, and so did half of the South Side. On a weekday you cannot get to the counter. My mother used to buy her calico from a man with a cart.

tales.title: Second Presbyterian
text: Our church on Wabash Avenue is built of stone with black flecks in it, bitumen they call it, and people call it the Spotted Church. The sermon this morning was on the parable of the talents and went on for an hour and ten minutes.
The minister prays for the city every Sunday. This morning he prayed for rain. Everyone in the pews said amen louder than I have heard them say anything.

tales.title: The State Street cars
text: I ride the State Street horse car to the shop every morning. Five cents, and you stand on the back platform with the smokers if there is no seat. The car runs on iron rails laid in the street, and two horses can pull forty people in it where they could not pull ten in a wagon through the mud.

The driver stands out on the front platform in all weathers with the reins and a brake handle. In January you see the frost on his whiskers. They run them on Sunday too, which some of the ministers do not like. Everybody else does.

tales.title: Last night's fire
text: Did you see it last night? The West Side, by Canal Street, a planing mill went up about eleven and took four blocks of lumber and houses with it, all the way from Van Buren to Adams. I went over the bridge to watch. Half the city did.

Every engine in the city was there, and they fought it all night with the wind pushing it north. The firemen were black to the eyes this morning, asleep on the hose carts. Some of the engines were damaged and the hose is burnt. I hope there is nothing tonight. They need a day.

tales.title: A clerk's wages
text: I am a clerk in a commission house on South Water Street: grain, flour, pork. Twelve dollars a week, which is good, and I sleep in a boarding house on Wabash with four other clerks in two rooms.

On Sunday we walk. You go out on the lake shore by the Water Works, or up to Lincoln Park where they are taking up the old cemetery, or you ride the car to the end of the line and back for ten cents and look at the houses. A man can see the whole city on a Sunday for a dime.

tales.title: Shoving lumber
text: I shove lumber on the South Branch. The schooners come in from Michigan and Wisconsin loaded to the gunwales with pine boards, and we carry it off on our shoulders and pile it in the yards, a board at a time, from six in the morning till dark.

There is more lumber in this city than in any city in the world, they say, and I believe it, because I have carried most of it. The yards run along the river for miles. On a dry day like this, when you light your pipe out there, the foreman watches you like a hawk.

tales.title: The yards
text: My brother works at the Union Stock Yards, out south past the city limits. He rides out on the cars before light. A hundred acres of pens, he says, and the cattle and the hogs come in on every railroad there is, and the packing houses take them in at one end and send out barrels of pork at the other.

He comes home smelling of it. My wife makes him leave his boots on the step. But he earns two dollars a day and he is never laid off in the winter, when the packing season comes. There are worse things to smell of than money.

tales.title: A working man's Sunday
text: Six days I work, and on the seventh I sit on my own step with my pipe and nobody tells me to move. That is my Sunday. Mass first, if the wife has her way, and then dinner, and then the step.
The children go off down to the river to see the boats, or out to the prairie at the end of the street to fly their kites. There is a wind today for kites. There has been a wind for a week.

tales.title: Kilgubbin
text: The respectable people call our part of the North Side by the river Kilgubbin, after a place in Cork, and they do not mean it kindly. Shanties and pigs and geese, they say. Well, the geese are good eating and the shanties were built by men who also built their houses.
My father came over in forty-nine with nothing but the clothes on him. Now I have a house of my own on a lot I pay for by the month. It is a small house. But it is mine and it is in America.

tales.title: Holy Family
text: The church of the Holy Family on Twelfth Street is the biggest church in the city, they say, built by the Jesuits for the Irish of the West Side out of our pennies. The priest says it holds four thousand and on a Sunday morning it is full twice over.
There is a school beside it now. My children go. They learn to read in English and to say their prayers in Latin, and they come home and tell me what everything means, as if I did not know.

tales.title: The cows on DeKoven Street
text: Down our street there are houses with a barn behind and a cow in it, and the women sell the milk to the neighbours. You pay a few cents and take your own can. It is cheaper than the milk wagon and you can see the cow you are getting it from.

The barns are full of hay for the winter now, and the sheds of wood and coal, everything bone dry. My husband says a match in one of those alleys and the whole street would go. He says it every Sunday. Then he lights his pipe.

tales.title: The North Side
text: On the North Side you can live your whole life in German: the church, the bakery, the newspaper, the Turnverein, the beer garden on a Sunday with the band playing and the children running about under the trees. The Yankees think a Sunday afternoon with music and a glass of lager is the road to ruin.

My father was a cabinet maker in Baden and I am a cabinet maker on Clark Street, and I make more in a week here than he made in a month. I have a vote and a lot of my own. On Sunday I sit in the garden with my family and nobody tells me I am going to hell for it except the people across the river.

tales.title: The brewery wagon
text: I drive for a brewery on the North Side, and Sunday is our busy day, which some people find scandalous. The beer gardens want their kegs before three, when the band starts. The horses know the way better than I do.

More breweries in this city than I can count on two hands. Lager is a German drink and twenty years ago you could not buy it here. Now the Irish drink it, the Yankees drink it behind the curtains, and the temperance ladies stand on the corner and pray for me as I go by. I always tip my hat.

tales.title: On Milwaukee Avenue
text: We came from Norway in sixty-six, on a sailing ship to Quebec and then by the lakes. My husband had a cousin on Milwaukee Avenue and that was all we knew of America: one cousin and the name of a street.

Now there are thousands of us out there, Norwegians and Swedes and Danes, with our own churches and our own newspaper. The men work in the planing mills and on the ships. I keep house and take in two boarders, which pays the rent. In winter it is like home. In summer it is hotter than any place God meant people to live.

tales.title: Pilsen on the West Side
text: The Bohemians live south of the Irish on the West Side, by the lumber yards where the men work. We have our own church, St. Wenceslaus, and a hall for the singing society, and the old women still wear their headscarves to market.

My husband shoves lumber like the Irish and gets paid the same, which is not much. But in Bohemia we would never have owned a house. Here we have two rooms, a cellar and a garden with cabbages in it, and the cabbages are doing well in all this sun, if nothing else is.

tales.title: Quinn Chapel
text: Our church is Quinn Chapel, the African Methodist church. Before the war it was a station on the underground road: people hid in the basement on the way to Canada, and the congregation fed them and sent them on. Some of those people stayed and they are in the pews today.

There are not many of us in the city, a few thousand, most on the South Side by Clark Street. The men work as waiters and porters in the hotels and on the railroads, as barbers and coachmen. It is not a free country yet, not all the way. But it is freer than where my mother was born.

tales.title: My afternoon out
text: Every second Sunday I have from three o'clock until supper, and I walk. I go to see my sister, who is in service on Michigan Avenue, and we walk on the lake front and look at the ladies' bonnets and decide which ones we would buy.

The mistress is kind enough. I get three dollars a week and my keep, which is more than I would get in a lifetime at home, and I send half of it back to my mother in Galway. I have a new hat. I bought it myself. It has a ribbon.

tales.title: From the roof
text: If you climb up on our roof you can see the Court House cupola, and if you climb up the Court House, which they let you do if you ask the bellman nicely, you can see the whole city to the prairie and out over the lake.

The man up there watches for fires. When he sees smoke he rings the bell and taps out the district on a telegraph, and the engines go. He has been busy all week. He told me he has never seen it so dry. He said it like it was interesting, not frightening.

tales.title: Kites on the prairie
text: At the end of our street the houses stop and it is all prairie, and when the wind is up we fly our kites there. Mine is red paper on two sticks with a tail of rags.
Today the wind is so strong it nearly pulled me over. My brother let his go and it went over the houses and we ran after it but it was gone. Mother says it is in Indiana by now.

tales.title: The steam engine
text: When the fire bell rings we run to see the engine come out. The firemen jump on and the horses come out of the stalls by themselves and stand under the harness and it drops on them, and then they go, with the smoke coming out of the chimney on the engine and sparks and the bell going.
The one I like best is the Little Giant, on Maxwell Street. I am going to be a fireman. Mother says I am going to be a clerk.

tales.title: Dressmaking
text: I make dresses in a room over a shop on Clark Street. Every lady wants the new shape this year, with all the fullness drawn back and a bustle under it, and an overskirt looped up over the skirt, and three flounces at the hem, and trimming on all of it. Thirty yards of silk in one dress, some of them.

I work from seven to nine six days a week, with two girls under me. On Sunday I do not touch a needle. I sit in the window and watch the ladies go by in my dresses and see which of them are wearing them properly. Most are not.

tales.title: Meeting the trains
text: I drive an express wagon. On Sunday the trains still come in, and somebody has to take the trunks from the depot to the hotels, and that is me. The Sherman House, the Tremont, the new Palmer House.

There are six railroad depots in this city and no two of them are in the same place, so a man going from New York to California has to cross Chicago in a hack and his trunk has to cross in my wagon. I am in favour of it. I would be out of work if they ever built one big depot.

tales.title: The milk round
text: I am up at three. Down to the dairy, load the cans, and out by five, every day God sends, Sundays included, because a baby does not know what day it is.

The horse knows every stop. He stops at the door before I tell him and waits while I fill the jug and goes on again by himself. I could sleep on the seat and he would bring me home. Some mornings I think I have.

tales.title: Washday tomorrow
text: Tomorrow is Monday, and Monday is the wash. I will be up at four to fill the boiler, and with the cistern near dry the water comes from the hydrant at the corner, two buckets at a time, a dozen times over. The wash water does the floors after, and the floor water goes on the garden, what is left of it.

By eight o'clock the whole street will have its sheets out. In a summer like this one they are dry in an hour and grey again in two, from the dust off the road. I do not know why I trouble. Yes, I do. My mother would turn in her grave at a grey sheet.

tales.title: Four boarders
text: I keep four boarders, young men from the stores and the railroad offices, and I give them breakfast and supper and a clean bed, and they give me their board on Saturday, most weeks. They come in at all hours. One of them plays the flute. Sunday dinner is the only meal they all sit down to, and they eat as if they had been lost in the woods for a month.

One asked me last week if I would lower his board, since he is out so much. I said I would lower it when the price of flour came down. The summer has seen to it that it will not. He is still here. They always stay.

tales.title: Filling the lamps
text: I fill the lamps in the morning, in daylight, on the back step, and I trim the wicks and wipe the chimneys, and I never carry a lit lamp near a curtain. The papers are full of lamps. A girl on the next street knocked one over in August and her whole kitchen went up before her father could get the pail.

In a summer this dry you think about fire the way you think about the weather. You smell smoke and you go to the window. Last night half the street was out in the road in their nightclothes, watching the glow over the West Side. I did not sleep until it was out.

tales.title: The Saturday market
text: Yesterday I took my basket down to the market, where the farmers bring their wagons in from the country before light. Everything is dear this year. The potatoes are the size of walnuts and the farmers say the corn is half what it ought to be. Not a drop of rain since July. You can see it in their faces.

I bought what I could and carried it home on the horse car. A woman beside me had a live goose under her arm, and it bit the conductor. Nobody else was sorry. You have to laugh, in a summer like this one, or you would sit down in the road and cry.

tales.title: The sewing machine
text: In the spring I bought a sewing machine, a dollar down and a dollar a week, from the agent who came round with his catalogue. It sits in the front room by the window like a piece of the parlour. My husband says it is the best thing we own, which is a fine thing for him to say, since he cannot thread it.

I make the children's clothes on it now, and my own, and I take in plain sewing from the ladies on the next street: hems and sheets and pillow slips, at so much the piece. What took me a week by hand takes me an afternoon. With what it brings in I will have it paid for by Christmas.

tales.title: A letter home
text: My sister writes every month from the old place and asks when I am coming home. I write back and tell her about the Water Tower, and the horse cars, and the marble store on State Street with the plate glass windows. I do not tell her about the mud in the spring or the smoke in the summer or the smell of the river.

She thinks Chicago is a city of palaces. Let her. In a way she is right. When I came here there was nothing on our street but two houses and a cow. Now there are thirty houses and the cow has gone, and I have a front step of my own to sit on of a Sunday.

tales.title: The new parlour
text: We moved into the new house on the Avenue in May, three storeys of brick with a stone front and a bay window, and I have done nothing since but furnish it. The parlour carpet came from New York. The piano came from Boston. The pier glass came from a shop on Lake Street and took four men to carry in.

My husband says a house is a machine for spending money in. He is not wrong. But when the gas is lit in the evening and the curtains are drawn, and my daughter is at the piano, I think it is the prettiest room in the city. I have asked the girl to keep the windows shut. The dust this summer gets into everything.

tales.title: The relief committee
text: On Thursdays I sit with the ladies of the church sewing committee, and we make up bundles for the poor: flannel petticoats, children's shirts, stockings, blankets for the winter. The Relief and Aid people give them out in the wards where the families are worst off.

There are women in this city, not a mile from my door, who have six children in one room and no coal laid by for the winter, and husbands who drink their wages on Saturday night. I did not know that when I came here as a bride. I know it now. I cannot do much. I can sew.

tales.title: Sunday errands
text: On Sunday I am sent on all the errands, because my brothers are at the river and my sister is too little. This morning it was to the druggist for my mother's headache powders, and then to my aunt's on Clark Street with a pie, and then back for the dish.

The whole city smells of smoke today from last night's fire. My aunt says it is a judgement. My mother says it is the dry weather. The druggist says it is bad for trade, because nobody comes out when the wind is like this. I think it is all three.

tales.title: The high school
text: I go to the public school, and next year, if I pass the examination, to the high school on the West Side, where they teach Latin and algebra and the natural sciences. My father did not go to school after he was ten. He wants us to go as long as we can.

The examination is in the spring. I study at the kitchen table after supper with the lamp turned up, and my mother sits across from me with her mending and asks me questions out of the book. She does not know the answers. She pretends she does, so that I will not stop.

tales.title: The water in the tap
text: We have a tap in the yard now, and the water comes out of it clear, and Papa says it comes all the way from out under the lake, two miles, through a tunnel, and up the tall tower on the North Side. I asked how the water knows to come here. He said the engines push it.

I went with my brother to see the tower. It is like a castle in a story, all white stone and little windows, and there is a pipe up the middle of it as tall as a church. I put my ear on the wall to hear the water. My brother said I was silly. Then he did it too.

tales.title: The bell
text: The bell goes dong, dong. Big bell. Up high.
Then the horses go fast. Clatter clatter. I wave at the horses. Mama holds my hand very tight.

tales.title: The kitty
text: We have a kitty. She is grey. She sleeps on the step in the sun.
I pat her soft. She goes purr. Then she goes away. She always goes away.

tales.title: The cart
text: The man has a cart. The horse is brown. It says neigh.
The man gave me an apple. A red one. I ate it all up. Not the middle.

tales.title: Bread
text: Mama makes bread. It goes in the oven. It smells good.
I had the end. It was hot. I blew on it. Then I ate it.

a: Never better, if you believe the Board of Trade, and they believe it themselves, which is what matters. The grain comes in on the railroads from the whole West and goes out by the lake, and every bushel of it pays somebody in this city a cent.
They said the same in fifty-seven, and the banks broke. I keep a little gold in the house. But a city of three hundred thousand that was a swamp forty years ago is not going to stop now.
A war, a panic, or the Lord's own hand. I do not expect any of them before Christmas.

No rain worth the name since the beginning of July. The wells are low, the grass is brown, and the wind has been blowing hot out of the southwest for a week. The leaves fell in September without turning.

In a city built of pine? The sidewalks are pine, the houses are pine with tar roofs, and there are lumber yards and planing mills and hay barns everywhere. There was a fire nearly every night this week. Last night's burned four blocks on the West Side.
That they are tired. They worked all night and half the day on that fire and some of the hose was burnt. They have seventeen steam engines for a city this size. I wish they had thirty.

The Palmer House, at State and Monroe. Mr. Potter Palmer built it and opened it two weeks ago. Seven or eight storeys, and a room for every day of the year and then some, with marble everywhere and gas in every room.

The man who owns State Street, or most of it. He made his money in dry goods, sold the store to Field and Leiter, and put his money into lots. He married a young lady from Kentucky last year, very handsome. The hotel was his wedding present to her, people say.

asks.q: What is the fashion this year?
a: Everything drawn back. The skirt is flat in front and all the fullness goes behind, over a bustle, with an overskirt looped up on top and flounces at the hem. Colours are strong this year: purples, deep greens, the browns they call bismarck. A small hat tipped forward, with flowers.
Comfortable! You sit on the edge of a chair and you go through doors sideways. But it is very becoming when you walk, and walking is what Sunday is for.
A dressmaker on Clark Street makes mine, from a picture in the Bazar. She grumbles about the yards of trimming and charges me for every one of them.

asks.q: What do ladies do on a Sunday afternoon?
a: Walk, and call. You leave cards at the houses of the people you know, and receive the people who know you. You talk about the sermon, the weather, the new hotel, the price of coal, the minister's wife's bonnet.

Today, the fire. Everyone saw the glow last night and everyone has an opinion on the Fire Department. Mrs. Jones's husband says it is all the fault of the city council. Mr. Jones says that about everything.

asks.q: How do I get across the city?
a: Take a horse car. The State Street cars run north and south from Lake Street to the south end, the Madison Street cars run west, the Randolph Street cars too, and on the North Side the Clark Street cars go up to Lincoln Park. Five cents.

Over the bridges, unless one of them is swung for a boat, in which case you wait, or go round by the tunnel at LaSalle Street or Washington. You will get used to it. Every Chicagoan has lost a quarter of his life at a swung bridge.

From the old country, like everybody. You will not meet many in this city who were born in it, except the children. Half of us came from across the water and the other half from New York and New England.

Because there was work, and land you could buy by the month, and a man was what he could do, not who his father was. That is the theory. It is not always the practice. But it is truer here than anywhere I have been.

asks.q: What do you do for work?
a: Whatever pays. This year I am in a lumber yard on the South Branch, carrying boards off the schooners. Last winter I was in a packing house. Before that I dug the sewers when they raised the streets.
A dollar and a half a day, two in the busy season. Rent is eight dollars a month for three rooms. My wife takes in sewing. We get by, and we have put by a little, in the savings bank on Clark Street.
On a Sunday I sit. I have earned it.

asks.q: Did you see the fire last night?
a: From the roof. It was over on the West Side, by Canal and Clinton, a planing mill and then everything round it, lumber and sheds and houses. The sky was red from one end to the other. You could read a newspaper by it on the North Side.
Not that I heard. Some firemen were burnt about the face, and they lost hose. Four blocks gone. It is out now, but they say it is still smoking in the ruins.
It happens every week. The trick is it happening where the engines can get at it.

asks.q: Which church do you go to?
a: Holy Family, on Twelfth Street, the Jesuits' church. It is the biggest church in the city. There is a Mass every hour on a Sunday morning, and still they stand at the back.
For the West Side Irish it is round the corner. For my cousin on the North Side it is a long walk, but she goes to St. Patrick's when her feet hurt.

asks.q: Is there music somewhere this afternoon?
a: In every beer garden on the North Side. A band plays, the families sit at the long tables under the trees, the children run about. You drink a glass of lager, you eat a sausage, you sing if you know the words.

more.q: Is that allowed on a Sunday?
a: The Yankee ministers say no. The law says the saloons should close. The police say nothing, because half of them are drinking in the garden. It is a quiet glass with your family. What harm is there in it?

It is a good place. The mistress is fair and the master is hardly home. There is a cook, and me, and a girl who comes in to do the washing. I have a room under the roof with a window that looks at the lake.

more.q: What do you do on your afternoon?
a: Walk with the other girls, and look in the windows on State Street, and buy a paper of sweets. On a fine day we go to the lake front and the young men try to talk to us. We let them, sometimes.

asks.q: What do you want to be?
a: A fireman. Or a driver on the horse cars. Or a clerk in a big store on State Street with a black coat and a gold watch chain. My father says a clerk, my mother says a priest, and my sister says a fool.

more.q: Have you seen the fire engines?
a: Last night I ran all the way to the West Side to see them, and my father gave me a whipping when I got home. It was worth it. You should hear the engines when they are going full: they shake.
Fire company. Tom is the engine and I am the horses and the little ones are the fire. You have to put them out.
The engine, always. That is the rule.
The company's horse, but I feed him and water him and talk to him all day, so he is mine in every way but the paper. He is called Dan. He is eleven years old and he knows the round better than I do.

more.q: Does he mind working on a Sunday?
a: He minds the dust. Look at his eyes. This summer has been hard on everything that breathes.

asks.q: How long have you been in Chicago?
a: Since before the war. I came up the river from Missouri and stayed, because there was work in the hotels and there were people here who would not send me back. Some of them hid people in their cellars when it was a crime to.
We vote now. Last year was the first time. I walked to the polls with my hat in my hand like I was going to church. Nobody stopped me. That is a different country from the one I was born in.

Ships. I was a sailor out of Bergen, and the lake schooners want men who know the work. In summer I sail lumber down from Michigan, in winter, when the lake freezes, I work in a planing mill on the North Branch.
In the winter, never. It is colder here than Bergen. In the summer, when it is like this, hot and dry and the dust in everything, yes.

Bohemians, mostly, on our street, and Irish round the corner, and Germans on the next street over, and every one of us thinks the others are a little strange. The children do not care. They play together and fight together and speak English to each other.
Enough for the market. My children speak it better than Czech now, which their grandmother says is a sin.

asks.q: How did you learn your trade?
a: From my mother, who learned it from hers, and then four years with a dressmaker in New York, threading needles and pressing seams and never being allowed to touch the good silk.
For a woman, it is one of the few. I keep myself, which is more than many married women can say they do. My eyes are going, though. The gas is not good to sew by.

cheerful.name: Cheerful
lines: {He} answers as if you were an old friend.

devout.name: Devout
lines: {He} touches something at {his} throat before {he} answers.
{He} answers gently, as if in church.
{He} pauses, as though asking a blessing.

dreamy.name: Dreamy
lines: {He} gazes off for a moment first.
{He} answers as if remembering a dream.
{He} takes a moment to come back to you.

earnest.name: Earnest
lines: {He} nods slowly and gives it proper thought.
{He} looks straight at you as {he} answers.

fiery.name: Fiery
lines: {He} jabs a finger to make {his} point.

gloomy.name: Gloomy
lines: {He} answers heavily, as if it costs {him}.

proud.name: Proud
lines: {He} answers as if it were obvious.

shrewd.name: Shrewd
lines: {He} answers as if striking a bargain.

shy.name: Shy
lines: {He} looks down, then up at you.

talkative.name: Talkative
lines: {He} has been waiting for someone to ask.
{He} settles in for a good long talk.
{He} is off before you finish the question.
{He} leans in, delighted to tell you.

wary.name: Wary
lines: {He} glances about first, then lowers {his} voice.

wry.name: Wry
lines: {He} smiles at one corner of {his} mouth.
{He} gives you a long, amused look.
